claim: Cells increase microtubule dynamics to make large rearrangements to their microtubule cytoskeleton during cell division.
source: Cells increase microtubule dynamics to make large rearrangements to their microtubule cytoskeleton during cell division.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell biology presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Changes in microtubule dynamics are essential for the formation and function of the mitotic spindle.
source: Changes in microtubule dynamics are essential for the formation and function of the mitotic spindle, and misregulation can lead to aneuploidy and cancer.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about mitotic spindle function.

claim: Misregulation of microtubule dynamics can lead to aneuploidy and cancer.
source: Changes in microtubule dynamics are essential for the formation and function of the mitotic spindle, and misregulation can lead to aneuploidy and cancer.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about the consequences of microtubule misregulation.

claim: CKAP2 lowers the critical tubulin concentration 100-fold.
source: Using in vitro reconstitution assays we show that the mitotic spindle protein Cytoskeleton-Associated Protein 2 (CKAP2) has a strong effect on nucleation of microtubules by lowering the critical tubulin concentration 100-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro reconstitution assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: CKAP2 increases the apparent rate constant ka of microtubule growth by 50-fold.
source: CKAP2 increases the apparent rate constant ka of microtubule growth by 50-fold and increases microtubule growth rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of microtubule growth kinetics presented in the manuscript.

claim: CKAP2 increases microtubule growth rates.
source: CKAP2 increases the apparent rate constant ka of microtubule growth by 50-fold and increases microtubule growth rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from microtubule growth assays.

claim: CKAP2 strongly suppresses catastrophes.
source: In addition, CKAP2 strongly suppresses catastrophes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of catastrophe frequencies presented in the manuscript.

claim: CKAP2 is the most potent microtubule growth factor to date.
source: Our results identify CKAP2 as the most potent microtubule growth factor to date.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the experimental data from this study with previously published data on other microtubule growth factors.

claim: During mitosis, cells build mitotic spindles to faithfully segregate their chromosomes.
source: During mitosis, cells build mitotic spindles to faithfully segregate their chromosomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitosis.

claim: Assembling mitotic spindles requires a complete rearrangement of the microtubule cytoskeleton, which is driven by the concerted action of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) and motor proteins.
source: Assembling mitotic spindles requires a complete rearrangement of the microtubule cytoskeleton, which is driven by the concerted action of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) and motor proteins (Kapoor, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Microtubule turnover increases significantly in mitosis resulting from increased microtubule nucleation.
source: Microtubule turnover increases significantly in mitosis resulting from increased microtubule nucleation (Piehl et al., 2004) in combination with shorter microtubule lifetimes (Saxton et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microtubule turnover increases significantly in mitosis in combination with shorter microtubule lifetimes.
source: Microtubule turnover increases significantly in mitosis resulting from increased microtubule nucleation (Piehl et al., 2004) in combination with shorter microtubule lifetimes (Saxton et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: XMAP215/chTOG and TPX2 have been implicated as two major factors in nucleation.
source: XMAP215/chTOG and TPX2 have been implicated as two major factors in nucleation (Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: XMAP215/chTOG family members are the only protein shown to speed up microtubule growth by more than a factor of 3 in in vitro assays.
source: In addition, XMAP215/chTOG family members are the only protein shown to speed up microtubule growth by more than a factor of 3 in in vitro assays (Brouhard et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Microtubules nucleate primarily from centrosomes as well as several centrosome-independent microtubule nucleation pathways aided by γ-tubulin ring complexes (γ-TURCs).
source: Microtubules nucleate primarily from centrosomes as well as several centrosome-independent microtubule nucleation pathways aided by γ-tubulin ring complexes (γ-TURCs) (Petry and Vale, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The γ-TURC only weakly increases microtubule nucleation and is thought to require activation of the complex itself or the help of MAPs like the microtubule polymerase XMAP215/chTOG or the nucleation factor TPX2.
source: Notably, the γ-TURC only weakly increases microtubule nucleation and is thought to require activation of the complex itself or the help of MAPs like the microtubule polymerase XMAP215/chTOG or the nucleation factor TPX2 (Consolati et al., 2020; Kollman et al., 2010; Moritz et al., 1995; Thawani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Cells lacking chTOG still have microtubules present.
source: Given the robustness of spindle assembly as well as the presence of microtubules in cells lacking chTOG (Gergely et al., 2003), TPX2 (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012), and γ-tubulin (Strome et al., 2001), it seems likely that additional factors can promote microtubule formation in spindles.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cells lacking TPX2 still have microtubules present.
source: Given the robustness of spindle assembly as well as the presence of microtubules in cells lacking chTOG (Gergely et al., 2003), TPX2 (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012), and γ-tubulin (Strome et al., 2001), it seems likely that additional factors can promote microtubule formation in spindles.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cells lacking γ-tubulin still have microtubules present.
source: Given the robustness of spindle assembly as well as the presence of microtubules in cells lacking chTOG (Gergely et al., 2003), TPX2 (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012), and γ-tubulin (Strome et al., 2001), it seems likely that additional factors can promote microtubule formation in spindles.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Additional factors beyond chTOG, TPX2, and γ-tubulin can promote microtubule formation in spindles.
source: Given the robustness of spindle assembly as well as the presence of microtubules in cells lacking chTOG (Gergely et al., 2003), TPX2 (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012), and γ-tubulin (Strome et al., 2001), it seems likely that additional factors can promote microtubule formation in spindles.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited observations about cells lacking known microtubule factors.

claim: CKAP2 is an intrinsically disordered protein.
source: The Cytoskeleton-Associated Protein 2 (CKAP2) is an intrinsically disordered protein (Figure 1a) that localizes to centrosomes and mitotic spindles during cell division (Seki and Fang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by disorder prediction shown in Figure 1a and cited work.

claim: CKAP2 localizes to centrosomes and mitotic spindles during cell division.
source: The Cytoskeleton-Associated Protein 2 (CKAP2) is an intrinsically disordered protein (Figure 1a) that localizes to centrosomes and mitotic spindles during cell division (Seki and Fang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CKAP2 expression and phosphorylation states are tightly regulated throughout the cell cycle.
source: CKAP2 expression and phosphorylation states are tightly regulated throughout the cell cycle.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent sentences that cite specific regulatory mechanisms.

claim: During G1 interphase, CKAP2 expression is at the detection level and increases at the onset of mitosis.
source: During G1 interphase, CKAP2 expression is at the detection level and increases at the onset of mitosis (Seki and Fang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CKAP2 is regulated by distinct phosphorylation events between different mitotic stages.
source: CKAP2 is regulated by distinct phosphorylation events between different mitotic stages (Hong et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) marks CKAP2 through a conserved, N-terminal KEN-box motif for degradation at the end of mitosis.
source: The anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) marks CKAP2 through a conserved, N-terminal KEN-box motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) for degradation at the end of mitosis to eliminate all CKAP2 from the newly formed daughter cells (Hong et al., 2007; Seki and Fang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing the KEN-box motif.

claim: The primary amino acid sequence of CKAP2 is poorly conserved compared to other MAPs like TPX2 and chTOG.
source: The primary amino acid sequence of CKAP2 is poorly conserved compared to other MAPs like TPX2 and chTOG and does not contain any known microtubule-binding domains (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: CKAP2 does not contain any known microtubule-binding domains.
source: The primary amino acid sequence of CKAP2 is poorly conserved compared to other MAPs like TPX2 and chTOG and does not contain any known microtubule-binding domains (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: About half the CKAP2 protein consists of the CKAP2_C domain (IPR029197).
source: About half the protein consists of the CKAP2_C domain (IPR029197), that defines the CKAP2 family.
evidence: This claim is based on domain analysis of the protein sequence.

claim: Like TPX2, CKAP2 is predicted to be highly intrinsically disordered in solution.
source: Like TPX2, CKAP2 is predicted to be highly intrinsically disordered in solution, and both proteins are significantly enriched in lysines (CKAP2 ~10%, TPX2 ~13%), likely to facilitate interactions with the negatively charged C-terminal tails of tubulin.
evidence: This claim is based on disorder prediction analysis.

claim: CKAP2 is significantly enriched in lysines (~10%).
source: Like TPX2, CKAP2 is predicted to be highly intrinsically disordered in solution, and both proteins are significantly enriched in lysines (CKAP2 ~10%, TPX2 ~13%), likely to facilitate interactions with the negatively charged C-terminal tails of tubulin.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of the protein.

claim: TPX2 is significantly enriched in lysines (~13%).
source: Like TPX2, CKAP2 is predicted to be highly intrinsically disordered in solution, and both proteins are significantly enriched in lysines (CKAP2 ~10%, TPX2 ~13%), likely to facilitate interactions with the negatively charged C-terminal tails of tubulin.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of the protein.

claim: The lysine enrichment in CKAP2 and TPX2 likely facilitates interactions with the negatively charged C-terminal tails of tubulin.
source: Like TPX2, CKAP2 is predicted to be highly intrinsically disordered in solution, and both proteins are significantly enriched in lysines (CKAP2 ~10%, TPX2 ~13%), likely to facilitate interactions with the negatively charged C-terminal tails of tubulin.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of lysine enrichment.

claim: About 60% of the CKAP2 protein sequence is predicted to be intrinsically disordered.
source: About 60% of the CKAP2 protein sequence is predicted to be intrinsically disordered (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on disorder prediction analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 45% of CKAP2 is disordered in solution as measured by circular dichroism.
source: We performed circular dichroism (CD) to confirm this prediction. Indeed, we find 45% of CKAP2 to be disordered in solution (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental CD data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 17% of CKAP2 contains turns as measured by circular dichroism.
source: Another 17% of the protein contains turns, 30% β-sheets, and 8% α-helices.
evidence: This claim is based on CD spectroscopy data.

claim: 30% of CKAP2 contains β-sheets as measured by circular dichroism.
source: Another 17% of the protein contains turns, 30% β-sheets, and 8% α-helices.
evidence: This claim is based on CD spectroscopy data.

claim: 8% of CKAP2 contains α-helices as measured by circular dichroism.
source: Another 17% of the protein contains turns, 30% β-sheets, and 8% α-helices.
evidence: This claim is based on CD spectroscopy data.

claim: Secondary structure prediction methods and AlphaFold predict α-helices for the ordered CKAP2 segments.
source: Interestingly, secondary structure prediction methods as well as AlphaFold predict α-helices for the ordered CKAP2 segments (Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on computational predictions and cites AlphaFold.

claim: CD data show β-sheets as the main secondary structure element for CKAP2 in solution, in contrast to predictions.
source: In contrast, our CD data predominantly show β-sheets as the main secondary structure element for CKAP2 in solution.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental CD data that contrasts with computational predictions.

claim: The measured disorder and secondary structure composition in solution for CKAP2 could change upon phosphorylation or interaction with tubulin, microtubules, or other binding partners.
source: Notably, the measured disorder and secondary structure composition in solution for CKAP2 could change upon phosphorylation or interaction with tubulin, microtubules, or other binding partners as it has been shown for many intrinsically disordered proteins (Uversky, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins, supported by a citation.

claim: At physiological tubulin levels (8 µM), increasing amounts of CKAP2 cause dose-dependent increase in light scattering and apparent absorbance (turbidity).
source: At physiological tubulin levels (8 µM), increasing amounts of CKAP2 cause dose-dependent increase in light scattering and apparent absorbance (turbidity).
evidence: This claim is supported by turbidity assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: At higher concentrations of CKAP2, turbidity continued to increase indicating that more microtubules are assembled faster.
source: At higher concentrations of CKAP2 turbidity continued to increase (Figure 1E) indicating that more microtubules are assembled faster.
evidence: This claim is based on turbidity data shown in Figure 1E and interpretation of the results.

claim: Increased microtubule bundling likely contributes to the measured turbidity effect.
source: In addition, increased microtubule bundling likely contributes to the measured effect.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential contributing factor to the observed turbidity.

claim: CKAP2 increased turbidity at 4°C, a temperature where tubulin does not form polymers and preformed microtubules depolymerize quickly in the absence of any stabilizers.
source: Furthermore, CKAP2 increased turbidity at 4°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), a temperature where tubulin does not form polymers and preformed microtubules depolymerize quickly in the absence of any stabilizers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and established knowledge about tubulin behavior at 4°C.

claim: Neither the mNeonGreen (mNG) nor the 6-His affinity tag had any impact on the ability of CKAP2 to aid microtubule formation.
source: Neither the mNeonGreen (mNG) nor the 6-His affinity tag had any impact on the ability of CKAP2 to aid microtubule formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: At 8 µM tubulin and in the presence of CKAP2, observation of individual growth events was only possible at very low CKAP2 concentrations (≤50 nM) due to high levels of spontaneous nucleation beyond that point.
source: At 8 µM tubulin, the lower end of estimated cellular tubulin concentrations and in the presence of CKAP2, observation of individual growth events was only possible at very low CKAP2 concentrations (≤50 nM) due to high levels of spontaneous nucleation beyond that point.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from TIRF microscopy assays.

claim: The microtubule growth rate increased linearly with CKAP2 at concentrations ≤50 nM.
source: The microtubule growth rate increased linearly with CKAP2 at these concentrations (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Microtubules polymerized with an apparent assembly rate constant (ka) of 2.6 ± 0.06 dimers μM−1 s−1 in controls.
source: Microtubules polymerized with an apparent assembly rate constant (ka) of 2.6 ± 0.06 dimers μM−1 s−1 in controls and 142 ± 3.3 dimers μM−1 s−1 in the presence of 500 nM CKAP2, representing a 54-fold increase in ka (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements of microtubule growth kinetics.

claim: Microtubules polymerized with an apparent assembly rate constant (ka) of 142 ± 3.3 dimers μM−1 s−1 in the presence of 500 nM CKAP2.
source: Microtubules polymerized with an apparent assembly rate constant (ka) of 2.6 ± 0.06 dimers μM−1 s−1 in controls and 142 ± 3.3 dimers μM−1 s−1 in the presence of 500 nM CKAP2, representing a 54-fold increase in ka (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements of microtubule growth kinetics.

claim: 500 nM CKAP2 causes a 54-fold increase in ka compared to controls.
source: Microtubules polymerized with an apparent assembly rate constant (ka) of 2.6 ± 0.06 dimers μM−1 s−1 in controls and 142 ± 3.3 dimers μM−1 s−1 in the presence of 500 nM CKAP2, representing a 54-fold increase in ka (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements and calculation from the data.

claim: Members of the XMAP215/chTOG family of microtubule polymerases achieve about fivefold maximal increase in ka.
source: By comparison, members of the XMAP215/chTOG family of microtubule polymerases achieve about fivefold maximal increase in ka (Brouhard et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work for comparison.

claim: 125 nM CKAP2 causes a 42-fold increase in ka.
source: We observed a 42-fold increase in ka for 125 nM CKAP2.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements of microtubule growth kinetics.

claim: Increasing the CKAP2 concentration beyond 500 nM did not further increase growth rates.
source: Increasing the CKAP2 concentration beyond 500 nM did not further increase growth rates.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from growth rate measurements.

claim: CKAP2 has about a threefold effect on the tubulin off-rate kd.
source: We observe a smaller effect (~threefold) on the tubulin off-rate kd (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CKAP2 is able to shift the critical concentration (Cc) for microtubule elongation from 2.89 ± 0.12 to 0.02 ± 0.002 μM with 500 nM CKAP2.
source: From the growth curves in Figure 2C and the spontaneous nucleation we observe at quasi-physiological concentrations of CKAP2 and tubulin, it is apparent that CKAP2 is able to shift the critical concentration (Cc) for microtubule elongation into the low nanomolar range (from 2.89 ± 0.12 to 0.02 ± 0.002 μM with 500 nM CKAP2) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2F.

claim: At quasi-physiological tubulin levels, microtubules nucleated from seed templates faster in the presence of ≥25 nM CKAP2.
source: At quasi-physiological tubulin levels microtubules nucleated from seed templates faster in the presence of as ≥25 nM CKAP2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CKAP2 shows very strong promotion of templated nucleation even at 100-fold lower tubulin concentrations compared to controls.
source: When we explored a wider range of CKAP2 and tubulin concentrations, we found a very strong promotion of templated nucleation by CKAP2 even at 100-fold lower tubulin concentrations compared to controls (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleation data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, E.

claim: The tubulin concentration for the half-maximal probability to nucleate within 1 min is reduced from 6.85 ± 0.48 µM in controls to 0.05 ± 0.01 µM for 0.5 µM CKAP2-mNG.
source: The tubulin concentration for the half-maximal probability to nucleate within 1 min is reduced from 6.85 ± 0.48 µM in controls to 0.05 ± 0.01 µM for 0.5 µM CKAP2-mNG.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of nucleation probability data.

claim: CKAP2 facilitates templated nucleation from seeds at tubulin concentrations as low as 50 nM.
source: CKAP2 facilitates templated nucleation from seeds at tubulin concentrations as low as 50 nM.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from nucleation assays.

claim: CKAP2 dramatically increases spontaneous nucleation with a shift in critical tubulin concentration from 25.4 ± 1.7 to 0.25 ± 0.02 μM.
source: We found that CKAP2 dramatically increases spontaneous nucleation with a shift in critical tubulin concentration from 25.4 ± 1.7 to 0.25 ± 0.02 μM (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by spontaneous nucleation data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CKAP2 promotes both templated and spontaneous nucleation.
source: CKAP2 therefore promotes both templated and spontaneous nucleation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing effects on both types of nucleation.

claim: In the presence of CKAP2, the Cc of spontaneous nucleation, as well as nucleation from templates, are lowered up to 100-fold.
source: In the presence of CKAP2, the Cc of spontaneous nucleation, as well as nucleation from templates, are lowered up to 100-fold.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements of critical concentrations for nucleation.

claim: CKAP2 lowers catastrophe frequencies in a concentration-dependent manner, reducing them to near zero at 50 nM CKAP2.
source: We quantified this effect and determined that CKAP2 lowers catastrophe frequencies in a concentration-dependent manner, reducing them to near zero at 50 nM CKAP2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by catastrophe frequency data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the presence of higher concentrations of CKAP2, catastrophe frequency was at least an order of magnitude lower than in controls.
source: In the presence of higher concentrations of CKAP2, catastrophe frequency was at least an order of magnitude lower than in controls (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by catastrophe frequency data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, C.

claim: The cytoplasmic linker-associated proteins (CLASPs) are the only other family of MAPs with a comparable effect on microtubule catastrophes to CKAP2.
source: The only other family of MAPs with a comparable effect on microtubule catastrophes are the cytoplasmic linker-associated proteins (CLASPs) (Aher et al., 2018; Lawrence et al., 2018; Majumdar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on CLASPs for comparison.

claim: CKAP2 does not show any significant interaction with tubulin in solution using size exclusion chromatography.
source: Using size exclusion chromatography, we do not find any significant interaction of CKAP2 and tubulin in solution (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CKAP2 is able to recruit soluble tubulin to microtubules.
source: In contrast, CKAP2 is able to recruit soluble tubulin to microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing tubulin recruitment.

claim: Microtubule lattice-bound CKAP2 recruits free Atto-663 tubulin to GMPCPP microtubule seeds.
source: Microtubule lattice-bound CKAP2 recruits free Atto-663 tubulin to GMPCPP microtubule seeds (Figure 5b, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b, c.

claim: CKAP2 possesses a distinct microtubule lattice binding site as well as likely one or multiple tubulin-binding sites.
source: CKAP2 therefore possesses a distinct microtubule lattice as well as likely one or multiple tubulin-binding sites.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations of lattice binding and tubulin recruitment.

claim: Recruitment of tubulin by lattice-bound CKAP2 could play a role in promoting microtubule nucleation and growth.
source: Recruitment of tubulin by lattice-bound CKAP2 could therefore play a role in promoting microtubule nucleation and growth.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism of CKAP2 action.

claim: At low protein concentrations (6.5 nM), CKAP2 tracks microtubule ends.
source: Indeed, at low protein concentrations (6.5 nM), CKAP2 tracks microtubule ends (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At higher CKAP2 concentrations (12.5 nM), end tracking is obscured by lattice-binding reminiscent of end tracking behaviour observed for the microtubule nucleation factors DCX and TPX2.
source: At higher concentrations (12.5 nM) end tracking is obscured by lattice-binding reminiscent of end tracking behaviour observed for the microtubule nucleation factors DCX and TPX2 (Figure 5D; Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012, Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and comparison to cited work on DCX and TPX2.

claim: CKAP2 shows higher affinity to the dynamic microtubule lattice over the GMPCPP lattice, unlike TPX2.
source: CKAP2 shows higher affinity to the dynamic microtubule lattice over the GMPCPP lattice, unlike TPX2 (Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and comparison to cited work on TPX2.

claim: Similar to TPX2 and DCX, CKAP2 recognizes microtubule curvature.
source: Similar to TPX2 (Roostalu et al., 2015) and DCX (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012), CKAP2 recognizes microtubule curvature (Figure 5e, f), which is thought to correlate with the high-affinity-binding site of these proteins at the microtubule end (Bechstedt et al., 2014; Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e, f and comparison to cited work.

claim: Microtubule curvature recognition is thought to correlate with the high-affinity-binding site of nucleation factors at the microtubule end.
source: Similar to TPX2 (Roostalu et al., 2015) and DCX (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012), CKAP2 recognizes microtubule curvature (Figure 5e, f), which is thought to correlate with the high-affinity-binding site of these proteins at the microtubule end (Bechstedt et al., 2014; Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited work on other proteins.

claim: Members of the XMAP215/chTOG family display robust autonomous end tracking at all physiologically relevant concentrations and do not recognize lattice curvature.
source: In contrast, members of the XMAP215/chTOG family display robust autonomous end tracking at all physiologically relevant concentrations and do not recognize lattice curvature (Brouhard et al., 2008; Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on XMAP215/chTOG for comparison.

claim: CKAP2 does not catalyze the reverse reaction of microtubule growth (depolymerization).
source: We did not observe any depolymerization over ~10 hr (Figure 5g, h and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) when we incubated GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules with CKAP2 at concentrations as high as 1 µM, while controls without CKAP2 displayed an expected depolymerization rate of about 0.013 ± 0.003 µm/min (Figure 5g, h). CKAP2 does not catalyze the reverse reaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by depolymerization assay data shown in Figure 5g, h and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CKAP2 strongly reduces the tubulin off-rate.
source: On the contrary, CKAP2 strongly reduces the tubulin off-rate.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from depolymerization assays.

claim: Cellular concentrations of CKAP2 in Xenopus eggs have been measured at about 60 nM in conjunction with 8.5 µM tubulin.
source: Cellular concentrations of CKAP2 in Xenopus eggs have been measured at about 60 nM in conjunction with 8.5 µM tubulin (Wühr et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work measuring cellular concentrations.

claim: At quasi-physiological CKAP2 and tubulin concentrations (60 nM and 8 µM), CKAP2 has a strong effect on the microtubule growth rate (~fivefold).
source: At these quasi-physiological CKAP2 and tubulin concentrations (assuming 60 nM and 8 µM) CKAP2 has a strong effect on the microtubule growth rate (~fivefold) in our assays (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the manuscript applied to physiological concentrations.

claim: At quasi-cellular CKAP2 concentrations, templated nucleation is almost instantaneous.
source: Further, templated nucleation is almost instantaneous (Figure 3B) and spontaneous nucleation is detectable.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At quasi-cellular CKAP2 concentrations, spontaneous nucleation is detectable.
source: Further, templated nucleation is almost instantaneous (Figure 3B) and spontaneous nucleation is detectable.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Catastrophe frequency is approaching zero at quasi-cellular CKAP2 concentrations (60 nM).
source: Catastrophe frequency is approaching zero at this concentration regime (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In cells, CKAP2 could increase microtubule nucleation, growth rates, and suppress catastrophe.
source: Therefore, in cells, CKAP2 could increase microtubule nucleation, growth rates, and suppress catastrophe.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential cellular effects based on in vitro data.

claim: At quasi-cellular CKAP2 concentrations, the effects on microtubule dynamics in in vitro assays are not fully saturated.
source: Interestingly, at quasi-cellular CKAP2 concentrations, the effects on microtubule dynamics in our in vitro assays are not fully saturated.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the dose-response data from the experiments.

claim: Cells may be susceptible to increased levels of CKAP2 as observed in several types of cancer.
source: Hence, cells may be susceptible to increased levels of CKAP2 as they have been observed in several types of cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that effects are not saturated at cellular concentrations.

claim: The CKAP2 used in this study was purified from E. coli likely in an unphosphorylated state.
source: Notably, we purify CKAP2 from E. coli likely in an unphosphorylated state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression system used.

claim: At full biochemical capacity of CKAP2, a 100-fold increase in spontaneous and templated nucleation was observed.
source: At full biochemical capacity of CKAP2, we observed a 100-fold increase in spontaneous and templated nucleation as well as a 54-fold increase in apparent tubulin on rate ka, and a complete suppression of microtubule catastrophe.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: At full biochemical capacity of CKAP2, a 54-fold increase in apparent tubulin on rate ka was observed.
source: At full biochemical capacity of CKAP2, we observed a 100-fold increase in spontaneous and templated nucleation as well as a 54-fold increase in apparent tubulin on rate ka, and a complete suppression of microtubule catastrophe.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: At full biochemical capacity of CKAP2, a complete suppression of microtubule catastrophe was observed.
source: At full biochemical capacity of CKAP2, we observed a 100-fold increase in spontaneous and templated nucleation as well as a 54-fold increase in apparent tubulin on rate ka, and a complete suppression of microtubule catastrophe.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: CKAP2 combines characteristics of microtubule nucleators (TPX2, DCX) as well as polymerases (XMAP215/chTOG) and anti-catastrophe factors (CLASPs).
source: Mechanistically, CKAP2 combines characteristics of microtubule nucleators (TPX2, DCX) as well as polymerases (XMAP215/chTOG) and anti-catastrophe factors (CLASPs).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of CKAP2's properties to other known MAPs.

claim: Like TPX2 and DCX, CKAP2 aids spontaneous nucleation.
source: Like TPX2 and DCX, CKAP2 aids spontaneous nucleation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from this study and comparison to known properties of TPX2 and DCX.

claim: TPX2, DCX, and CKAP2 all display end tracking behaviour at low concentrations as well as lattice curvature recognition.
source: All three proteins display end tracking behaviour at low concentrations as well as lattice curvature recognition.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from this study for CKAP2 and cited work for TPX2 and DCX.

claim: End tracking behavior and lattice curvature recognition seem to be a hallmark of microtubule nucleation factors and might point towards the structural nature of the nascent nucleus.
source: These characteristics seem to be a hallmark of microtubule nucleation factors and might point towards the structural nature of the nascent nucleus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on observed commonalities among nucleation factors.

claim: Similar to TPX2, CKAP2 is largely intrinsically disordered and dampens tubulin off-rates and microtubule dynamicity.
source: Similar to TPX2, CKAP2 is largely intrinsically disordered and dampens tubulin off-rates and microtubule dynamicity (Reid et al., 2016; Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from this study and comparison to cited work on TPX2.

claim: A potential mechanism for nucleation by CKAP2 is the stabilization of the nascent microtubule nucleus.
source: A potential mechanism for nucleation by CKAP2 is the stabilization of the nascent microtubule nucleus (Roostalu and Surrey, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism, supported by a citation to a general review.

claim: Similar to the CLASP anti-catastrophe factors, CKAP2 lowers the catastrophe frequency to virtually zero.
source: Similar to the CLASP anti-catastrophe factors, CKAP2 lowers the catastrophe frequency to virtually zero (Aher et al., 2018; Lawrence et al., 2018; Majumdar et al., 2018), allowing for continued microtubule growth even at nanomolar concentrations of tubulin.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from this study and comparison to cited work on CLASPs.

claim: CKAP2 allows for continued microtubule growth even at nanomolar concentrations of tubulin.
source: Similar to the CLASP anti-catastrophe factors, CKAP2 lowers the catastrophe frequency to virtually zero (Aher et al., 2018; Lawrence et al., 2018; Majumdar et al., 2018), allowing for continued microtubule growth even at nanomolar concentrations of tubulin.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from the manuscript.

claim: Other MAPs that stabilize the microtubule lattice like DCX, TPX2, and CLASPs, as well as stabilizing drugs like paclitaxel or GTP analogues like GMPCPP, do not severely impact the microtubule growth curve.
source: Other MAPs that stabilize the microtubule lattice like DCX (Moores et al., 2006), TPX2 (Reid et al., 2016), and CLASPs (Lawrence et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2016), as well as stabilizing drugs like paclitaxel (Zanic et al., 2013) or Guanosine-5'-triphosphate (GTP) analogues like GMPCPP (Hyman et al., 1992), do not severely impact the microtubule growth curve.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on these other factors.

claim: Lattice stabilization alone cannot account for the severe impact of CKAP2 on the apparent tubulin on rate ka.
source: Therefore, lattice stabilization alone cannot account for the severe impact of CKAP2 on the apparent tubulin on rate ka.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to other lattice-stabilizing factors.

claim: Unlike TPX2, DCX, and CLASPs, CKAP2 also acts, in part, like a polymerase.
source: Unlike TPX2, DCX, and CLASPs, CKAP2 also acts, in part, like a polymerase.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of CKAP2's properties to other MAPs.

claim: Similar to known polymerases of the XMAP215/chTOG family, microtubule-bound CKAP2 recruits tubulin and increases the association rate constant (ka) at the microtubule end.
source: Similar to known polymerases of the XMAP215/chTOG family, microtubule-bound CKAP2 recruits tubulin and increases the association rate constant (ka) at the microtubule end (Brouhard et al., 2008; Gard and Kirschner, 1987).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from this study and comparison to cited work on XMAP215/chTOG.

claim: CKAP2 is able to push microtubule growth to the physical limit as defined by diffusion of the tubulin dimer to the growing microtubule end.
source: In contrast to XMAP215/chTOG family members, CKAP2 is able to push microtubule growth to the physical limit as defined by diffusion of the tubulin dimer to the growing microtubule end (Odde, 1997; Zanic et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and comparison to theoretical limits cited in previous work.

claim: Unlike a polymerase, CKAP2 does not catalyze the reverse reaction of tubulin polymerization in the absence of tubulin substrates.
source: Unlike a polymerase, CKAP2 does not catalyze the reverse reaction of tubulin polymerization in the absence of tubulin substrates.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from depolymerization assays.

claim: CKAP2 either does not operate as a bona fide polymerase, or the depolymerase activity is masked by the lattice stabilization activity of CKAP2.
source: CKAP2 either does not operate as a bona fide polymerase, or the depolymerase activity is masked by the lattice stabilization activity of CKAP2.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential explanations for the observed behavior.

claim: In contrast to XMAP215/chTOG, CKAP2 does not interact with GDP tubulin in size exclusion chromatography experiments.
source: In contrast to XMAP215/chTOG, CKAP2 does not interact with GDP tubulin in size exclusion chromatography experiments.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from size exclusion chromatography.

claim: Microtubule growth in the presence of CKAP2 resembles that of microtubules grown in the presence of the slowly hydrolysable GTP analogue, GMPCPP.
source: In many ways, microtubule growth in the presence of CKAP2 resembles that of microtubules grown in the presence of the slowly hydrolysable GTP analogue, GMPCPP.
evidence: This is a comparison based on observed similarities in behavior.

claim: With GMPCPP, microtubules nucleate at nanomolar concentrations of tubulin and are relatively stable.
source: With GMPCPP, microtubules nucleate at nanomolar concentrations of tubulin and are relatively stable (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Hyman et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on GMPCPP.

claim: GMPCPP does not increase apparent on rate ka, unlike CKAP2.
source: However, GMPCPP does not increase apparent on rate ka, like CKAP2.
evidence: This is a comparison based on known properties of GMPCPP and experimental data on CKAP2.

claim: CKAP2 is about one third of the size of XMAP215/chTOG.
source: The protein is about one third of the size of XMAP215/chTOG, about half the size of CLASPs, and is lacking any known microtubule or tubulin-binding domains.
evidence: This is a comparison based on known protein sizes.

claim: CKAP2 is about half the size of CLASPs.
source: The protein is about one third of the size of XMAP215/chTOG, about half the size of CLASPs, and is lacking any known microtubule or tubulin-binding domains.
evidence: This is a comparison based on known protein sizes.

claim: The highly disordered nature of CKAP2 contributes to its ability to dynamically interact with the microtubule lattice as well as tubulin and impact microtubule assembly to an extreme extent.
source: We believe that the highly disordered nature of CKAP2 (Figure 1a, b) contributes to its ability to dynamically interact with the microtubule lattice as well as tubulin and impact microtubule assembly to an extreme extent.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of disorder.

claim: The advantage of disordered over folded domains is the absence of a structured, tight binding conformation to a substrate or intermediate state.
source: The advantage of disordered over folded domains is the absence of a structured, tight binding conformation to a substrate or intermediate state.
evidence: This is a general statement about properties of disordered proteins based on established knowledge.

claim: Lack of a fixed structure in CKAP2 would allow for fast molecular recognition of the tubulin dimer as well as for rapid unbinding.
source: In case of a microtubule growth factor, lack of a fixed structure would allow for fast molecular recognition of the tubulin dimer as well as for rapid unbinding, that is letting go of the dimer when incorporated (Uversky and Dunker, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional consequences of disorder, supported by a citation.

claim: Binding of CKAP2 to microtubules likely causes the adoption of a secondary structure of part of the protein.
source: Binding of CKAP2 to microtubules likely causes the adoption of a secondary structure of part of the protein.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins.

claim: Structural rearrangements upon binding could explain the lack of interaction with tubulin in solution in contrast to lattice-bound CKAP2.
source: Such structural rearrangements could explain the lack interaction with tubulin in solution in contrast to lattice-bound CKAP2.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed experimental results.

claim: Even small changes in microtubule assembly rates are correlated with increased levels of chromosomal instability (CIN) in cells.
source: Even small changes in microtubule assembly rates are correlated with increased levels of chromosomal instability (CIN) in cells (Ertych et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CIN can provide the high adaptation capability necessary for tumor initiation and progression.
source: CIN can provide the high adaptation capability necessary for tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about CIN and cancer.

claim: Reducing microtubule growth rates in cancer cells by chemical or genetic manipulation suppresses CIN.
source: Correspondingly, it has been shown that reducing microtubule growth rates in cancer cells by chemical or genetic manipulation suppresses CIN (Ertych et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Upregulation of CKAP2 as observed in many cancers could be directly responsible for CIN, and subsequently for aneuploidy, and malignancies.
source: Upregulation of a potent growth factor like CKAP2 as observed in many cancers could therefore be directly responsible for CIN, and subsequently for aneuploidy, and malignancies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of CKAP2 in cancer based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cells need to tightly regulate the expression and activity of a potent microtubule growth factor like CKAP2.
source: Cells need to tightly regulate the expression and activity of a potent microtubule growth factor like CKAP2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the potent effects of CKAP2 observed in the study.

claim: Known regulatory measures for CKAP2 include rapid degradation by APC as well as distinct phosphorylation and dephosphorylation events in between different stages of the cell cycle.
source: Known regulatory measures include rapid degradation by APC (Seki and Fang, 2007) as well as distinct phosphorylation and dephosphorylation events in between different stages of the cell cycle (Hong et al., 2008; Hong et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on CKAP2 regulation.

claim: Phosphorylation could alter the effects of CKAP2 on microtubule dynamics and tune CKAP2 functionality between nucleation, stabilization, and growth.
source: Phosphorylation could alter the effects of CKAP2 on microtubule dynamics and tune CKAP2 functionality between nucleation, stabilization, and growth.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The findings suggest an explanation for the observed CKAP2 knock-down spindle phenotypes.
source: Our results suggest an explanation for the observed CKAP2 knock-down spindle phenotypes and the oncogenic potential through the misregulation of microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to previously observed cellular phenotypes.

claim: The findings suggest an explanation for the oncogenic potential of CKAP2 through the misregulation of microtubule dynamics.
source: Our results suggest an explanation for the observed CKAP2 knock-down spindle phenotypes and the oncogenic potential through the misregulation of microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to the clinical relevance of CKAP2.

claim: Knock-down of CKAP2 in cells interferes with proper spindle assembly and often results in multipolar spindles and misaligned chromosomes.
source: Knock-down of CKAP2 in cells interferes with proper spindle assembly and often results in multipolar spindles and misaligned chromosomes (Case et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of CKAP2 promotes cancer formation.
source: Overexpression of CKAP2 promotes cancer formation (Guo et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2015) and correlates with severity of the disease (Hayashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of CKAP2 correlates with severity of cancer.
source: Overexpression of CKAP2 promotes cancer formation (Guo et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2015) and correlates with severity of the disease (Hayashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CKAP2 is a marker for the diagnosis and prognosis of several types of cancer.
source: Consequently, CKAP2 is a marker for the diagnosis and prognosis of several types of cancer (Hayashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CKAP2 has been previously described as a potential microtubule stabilizer in cells.
source: CKAP2 has been previously described as a potential microtubule stabilizer in cells (Jin et al., 2004; Tsuchihara et al., 2005), though it is not known whether CKAP2 directly binds to microtubules or how it affects microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It was not known whether CKAP2 directly binds to microtubules or how it affects microtubule dynamics prior to this study.
source: CKAP2 has been previously described as a potential microtubule stabilizer in cells (Jin et al., 2004; Tsuchihara et al., 2005), though it is not known whether CKAP2 directly binds to microtubules or how it affects microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This statement describes the knowledge gap that motivated the study.
